messages.subject: [statnet_help] ergm constraints argument freezes R
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am currently working on a network of about 70 students who have selected
each other for friendships. I specified the ergm such as this:

m9A1<-ergm(netA1 ~
             edges +
             mutual +
             absdiff('class') +
             gwesp(0.25, fixed = TRUE) +
             gwdsp(0.25, fixed = TRUE) +
             absdiff('Extraversion.weightedAvg.Self') +

             absdiff('Agreeableness.weightedAvg.Self') +

             absdiff('Conscientiousness.weightedAvg.Self') +

             absdiff('Stability.weightedAvg.Self') +

             absdiff('Openness.weightedAvg.Self') +
             nodematch('Gender') +
             nodematch('Race') +
             absdiff('Age') +
             absdiff('politicalviews') +
             nodematch('LT') +
             absdiff('RelativeAttractiveness') +
             absdiff('enjoydrinking'),
           constraints = ~bd(maxout = 5)
)


When I originally ran this model, it worked completely fine. However, a few
days later, whenever I try to run this code, my R freezes and I have to
restart my computer. When I remove the "constraints" argument, it works
just fine. I have tried updating my OS, updating R, updating RStudio,
updating statnet and yet the problem still persists. Is there any reason
why this may be happening?

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Comparing ergm coefficients
messages.body_plain:
Hi Zachary,

In principle, comparing ergm coefficients is much like comparing 
coefficients from logistic regression.  In general we don't say a 
coefficient is "more significant" if it's p-value is lower.  However, one 
would typically then be able to say that there is less uncertainty, 
because the CI for that coefficient will be tighter (since both the 
p-value and the CI depend on the same SE).

Keep in mind also that the magnitude (value) of a coefficient needs to be 
carefully interpreted.  The nodematch term, for example, takes two values 
(0 for no, 1 for yes), so the coefficient reflects how the odds of a tie 
changes across these two levels.  In contrast, the absdiff term will take 
as many values as there are levels for this attribute.  If there are, say, 
k levels, then the value of the absdiff coefficient will be multiplied by 
anything from 0 to k to determine the impact on the odds of a tie.  Even 
if the absdiff coefficient is smaller in value than the nodematch 
coefficient, the potential impact of the product of the coef x termvalue 
may still be larger.

hth,
Martina

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Comparing ergm coefficients
messages.body_plain:
Hi

I second Martina's comments with respect to the terms. You need to
think carefully about the units, and I think you are on the right
track:

The nodematch term essentially estimates the odds ratio between
within-group ties and between group ties (group=ethnicity, so it is a
nominal variable). The coeficient tells you, ceteris paribus, how much
more likely the within-group ties are (as opposed to between-group),
it is an odds-ratio.

The absdiff term essentially models log-odds of a tie as a linear
function of the absolute difference on some quantitiative node
covariate. In other words, the coefficent is also an odds-ratio, but
this time you measure how much more likely the ties are between the
nodes if the absolute difference of their covariate values increases
by 1. The value of the coefficient is therefore directly related to
the units in which your covariate is measrued.

In that sense these two coefficients are hard to compare directly. To
get a better grasp which one is more *substantively* significant you
may try computing what size of the absolute difference on your node
covariate seems to be associated with similar odds ratio as the ethnic
similarity. If in your ERGM results you see e.g.

absdiff  = -0.69
nodematch = 1.38

This means that same-ethnicity ties are exp(1.38) = 4 times more
likely than cross-ethnicity ties.
And that the for every unit increase in absolute difference on the
node covariate the odds of a tie exp(-0.69) = 0.5 so almost halved (or
2 times *less* likely).

Now, because 4 / 2 = 2 you could say that the different ethnicities of
people makes ties between them less likely by the same factor, as
being different on extraversion scale 2 units away. Whether or not a
difference of 2 units on extraversion scale is worth paying attention
to is a matter of the way how it was measured.


I hope this helps.


Best,
Michal

messages.body_plain:
Hi, Jesse -

/tl;dr: wrapping your input network(s) in as.edgelist.sna with the 
attrname argument set to the name of your edge attribute should do the 
trick.  See below for a longer explanation of why this is necessary.//
/

The issue you are running into is that when you pass a network object to 
an sna function, it has no way of knowing what attribute you want to use 
for edge values (since you could have many different edge value 
attributes on the same network object). Thus, your network gets coerced 
to an unvalued structure, which is then operated upon (here by degree).  
To be more precise, here's what happens "under the hood" in a typical 
sna function:

1. Input data gets to checked to see if it is in sna edgelist (or 
occasionally adjacency matrix) form.
2. If not, input data gets sent to as.edgelist.sna (or occasionally 
as.sociomatrix.sna) for coercion.
3. If needed, the data is coerced, and the coerced data is returned.
4. The function operates on the (possibly coerced) input data.

The upside of this is that these functions can take data in many 
different forms (some of which are very spartan), and operate in a 
mostly transparent fashion.  The downside is that that they cannot 
assume very much about what the input data will contain; network 
objects, in particular, can contain very rich metadata, and you need to 
explicitly pass this to the function in order to use it. (It may be 
worth noting here that sna predates network, and until recently did not 
depend on it, so we couldn't build in automagic network object-centric 
functionality without creating an extra dependency that we were trying 
to avoid.  Now that sna does depend on network, we may revisit this 
issue in future releases.)

In order to pass edge values to an sna function, the best way is usually 
to perform the coercion yourself.  Wrapping your network (or a list 
thereof) in as.edgelist.sna and using the "attrname" argument to set the 
attribute you would like to use for edge values will ensure that those 
values are extracted and then passed on to degree (or any other function 
of interest).  Telling degree to use the edge value information should 
then produce the desired results.  As noted above, you can store as many 
different edge value attributes as you like within a single network 
object, and then use this approach to "dial in" only the values that are 
relevant for your specific analysis.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

Hi, Shiran,

1) I was able to run the examples but I did not understand what is the difference between finding latent position models like this code: ergm(samplk.tot~edges+nodematch("group",diff=TRUE))  and ERGM models.

This model does not ask for a latent space: nodematch() is for exogenous grouping. If you request tofit="mle", the results should be identical to those from ergm().

A latent space fit, like

ergmm(samplik.tot~edges + euclidean(d=2, G=3))

would ask the package to find the groups in the network, whatever they may be.

2) How can I interoperate the summary of the model to latent positions?  is cluster affiliation of a node suggests it's role in the network?

I think that it for Euclidean distance, at least, it suggests is affiliation to a particular cohesive subgroup in the network.

3)I did understand that I can find clusters, but how can I explain the reason a node was classified to a certain cluster?
In k-means the centroids are the mean of  the features that I used in the model.

It's model-based clustering. See the Handcock, Raftery, and Tantrum (2007) paper.

4) I read the the classification is based on the Euclidean distance but I did not understand what are the coordinates that are used to determine the node's location in the Euclidean space.
I guess my question is: how does the algorithm classify nodes to clusters?

It estimates them, choosing (loosely) positions such that distances among them correspond to the relations.

5) In the social Euclidean space what do the coordinates represent? is it the probability of two members forming an edge?

Yes. Take a look at the papers referenced for the interpretation.

6) Also what does random effects mean regarding networks? is it like random effects in GLMM (a different interception or slop for each node)?

In a sense, yes. It might be easier to think of it as a latent propensity of each node to send and/or receive ties.

I hope this helps,
Pavel

Dear Frans,

I am relatively new to ERGMs and I am currently trying to fit a number of ego networks using the ergm.ego package. Some beginner?s questions:


1)      Is it possible (or even useful?) to calculate the AIC and BIC of ergm.ego model fits? It seems that the option was included in older versions, but it doesn?t seem to work anymore in the newer version (I am using version 0.3.0)?

For the inferential machinery used by ergm.ego, AIC and BIC are not straightforward. There are some equivalents, but they are not implemented yet.




2)      Options to add complex dependency terms (like gwdegree, gewesp & gwdesp) are not included in the package. Is this something that will be added in the future, or are these not included because these kind of terms are not relevant to model the characteristics of typical ego networks anyway?


These were not included because they cannot be identified when alter-alter ties are unobserved. The version for which they are is a work in progress.

Best Regards,
Pavel



Any help would be greatly appreciated.

Kind regards,

Frans Hermans
